questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the sources of uncertainty in geography named in the reading?
questions.why: The reading names three sources: stochastic processes, imperfect measurement, and working with samples rather than whole populations.

options: a variable that has been randomly sampled
any variable whose outcome involves uncertainty, whatever the source of that uncertainty
a variable with a normal distribution
a variable that changes over time
questions.why: Uncertainty can come from randomness, measurement or sampling. Any of them makes the outcome a random variable.

questions.q: A probability distribution built from 50 years of recorded summer temperatures is...
questions.why: Empirical distributions come straight from observed frequencies. Theoretical ones are defined mathematically from assumptions about the process.

questions.q: Which of these is a discrete variable?
options: Number of floods in a decade
questions.why: Discrete variables take countable values. Rainfall, elevation and distance are measured along a continuum.

questions.q: For a continuous variable like temperature, the probability of one exact value (say, exactly 88.000°F) is...
options: about 0, so we calculate probabilities over ranges
the height of the curve at that value
the same as for a discrete variable
questions.why: On a continuous distribution, probability is area under the curve, and a single point has no width, so you work with ranges.

questions.q: On a normal curve, the probability that an observation falls below a value is...
options: the height of the curve at that value
the area under the curve to the left of that value
the mean divided by the standard deviation
questions.why: Probability is area under the curve. Below a value means the area to the left.

questions.q: Why would a researcher fit a theoretical distribution to temperature data instead of only counting past days?
options: Theoretical distributions don't need any data
It lets you estimate probabilities for values that may not appear in the observed record
questions.why: A fitted distribution generalizes beyond the sample. It still needs parameters, such as the mean and standard deviation, estimated from the data.

questions.q: In estimation in sampling, the uncertainty comes mainly from...
options: random sampling variability: different samples give different estimates
questions.why: Each random sample gives a slightly different estimate. Confidence intervals quantify that variability.

questions.q: Comparing whether transportation mode differs across neighborhood types (categorical counts) would use...
questions.why: Chi-square tests work with categorical data and frequency counts. The t-tests compare means.

questions.q: Why does spatial pattern analysis need probability, even though we can see the map?
options: Completely random processes can still produce apparent clusters and gaps by chance
questions.why: You compare the observed pattern to what random arrangements produce, often with Monte Carlo simulation, before calling it a real pattern.

questions.q: OLS regression typically assumes that the residuals...
options: follow a normal distribution with constant variance
questions.why: That assumption is what allows confidence intervals and p-values. Spatial regression models relax the independence part.

questions.q: If you have data for every county in the US (the whole population), why might you still use statistical inference?
options: You never would; inference only applies to samples
The observed pattern is one possible realization of processes that contain randomness
Counties are always a sample of states
questions.why: Geographers often treat the observed arrangement as one outcome of a stochastic process, so they ask whether it reflects a systematic process or chance.
